children: Strap: Sustainability leaders say climate innovation must deliver commercial proof before enterprises commit to large-scale adoption

India Inc is moving beyond experimenting with climate technologies and placing greater emphasis on solutions that can demonstrate measurable business value, operational reliability and commercial scalability. That was the key takeaway from BW Businessworld’s panel discussion, ‘Climate Tech at Scale: What Does India Inc Need Beyond the Pilot?’, where leaders from banking, manufacturing, cooling and technology agreed that the next phase of climate innovation will be driven by enterprise adoption rather than successful pilots alone.

Moderated by Samir Shah, Managing Partner, Peak Sustainability Ventures, the session featured Manish Kumar, Head of ESG & CSR at ICICI Bank; Astrid Dias, Head of Sustainability at Voltas; Lovish Ahuja, Chief Sustainability Officer at Dalmia Bharat; and Hiran Prashanth, Director of Corporate Sustainability at HCL Tech.
Beyond The Pilot

Opening the discussion, Shah said scaling climate solutions requires a stronger partnership between startups, investors and corporates, arguing that innovation only creates impact when businesses adopt it across operations.
“Without scale, you are not going to achieve any of the proposed outcomes in climate,” said Samir Shah, Managing Partner, Peak Sustainability Ventures.

For ICICI Bank, climate technology is no longer a peripheral ESG initiative but an embedded business function. Kumar explained that the lender has created a dedicated startup ecosystem banking team that supports climate startups with both financing and industry access, helping them progress from early-stage development to commercial deployment.
“Technology has been a backbone of how we have really evolved as an organisation,” said ICICI Bank’s Manish Kumar, Head of ESG & CSR.

He added that the bank has introduced an end-to-end ESG reporting platform that gathers sustainability data directly from core banking systems, while atmospheric water generators across offices have reduced dependence on bottled water and improved resource circularity.

Voltas offered the perspective of a company operating in a warming climate, where rising temperatures simultaneously increase demand for cooling and the responsibility to improve efficiency. Dias said artificial intelligence is now helping consumers optimise electricity consumption through occupancy-based cooling, geolocation and usage analytics.

“We are in the business of cooling… climate change is an opportunity for us to increase sales, but it also becomes very difficult because emissions will ultimately go up,” said Voltas’ Astrid Dias, Head of Sustainability.
Dias noted that the industry continues to face a difficult balance between developing refrigerants with lower global warming potential and ensuring they remain safe for widespread consumer use.
Proving Commercial Value

For high-emitting industries, the discussion shifted from sustainability ambition to economic survival. Ahuja said cement manufacturing remains inherently carbon-intensive, making continuous technological improvement essential as India strengthens its carbon market framework.
“This is not a privilege. It’s not a matter of choice,” said Dalmia Bharat’s Lovish Ahuja, Chief Sustainability Officer, describing the role of climate technology in the cement industry.

He highlighted Dalmia Bharat’s renewable energy portfolio, where 46 per cent of electricity now comes from clean sources, while waste heat recovery contributes 22 per cent of captive power demand. The company has also replaced a significant share of conventional fuels with municipal solid waste, creating both cost and circularity benefits.

From the technology sector, Prashanth argued that digital tools are transforming sustainability management itself. Rather than replacing human expertise, artificial intelligence is removing the burden of manual reporting and data validation, allowing teams to focus on strategic interventions.
“Clean makes business sense,” said HCL Tech’s Hiran Prashanth, Director of Corporate Sustainability, adding that energy savings and operational efficiency directly strengthen business performance.

Asked what startups should build next, the panellists converged on practical industrial challenges: water innovation, low-grade waste heat recovery, safer refrigerants, carbon utilisation and circular waste management. Their message was consistent. The technologies that secure enterprise procurement will be those that solve real operational problems while delivering measurable commercial returns.
Ayoshi Mondal
BW Reporters The author is a Trainee Correspondent at BW Businessworld.
